posts.content:
A lot of what we ask AI to do has three or four possible answers.

A customer helpdesk sorts tickets into billing, technical or sales, and flags them as urgent or routine. An AI agent decides whether to act or ask a human. These are small decisions made thousands of times a day, and the standard tool for them is a large language model like ChatGPT or Claude.

But an LLM is a prediction engine, built for open-ended work. It writes, reasons and explains, and it produces the answer one token at a time, running the full model for each piece. Ask it a yes or no question and you get an elaborate explanation. That is by design, and you're literally paying for all that spiel you don't even need.

Take a support inbox with 2,000 tickets every morning. Some are easy. "I was charged twice this month" is billing. "The export button crashes the app" is technical. "What does the enterprise plan cost?" is sales. For tickets like these, a paragraph of reasoning adds nothing. You want the label.

The border issues pose a bigger problem. A customer complaint that says "I upgraded to Pro and the new features still aren't in my account" could be a failed payment, which is billing, or a feature that never switched on, which is technical. A chat model replies with a sentence: "This looks primarily like a billing concern, though there's a technical element too." If you force it to return one word, the answer gets short, but the uncertainty disappears. The double charge (definite) and the upgrade ticket (possible) both come back "billing," and the output shows no difference. You are also still running a full-size model for a job with three answers.

Asking for a confidence score doesn't solve this. LLMs predict text, then get tuned on which answers human raters preferred, not on whether the answer was right.

For jobs like this, Typesafe AI built a model called Jev. Jev returns a probability for each option plus a confidence score, with no sentence around it. The upgrade ticket might come back 62% technical and 38% billing, with low confidence. The double charge comes back billing with high confidence. Typesafe trains Jev on examples where the right answer is already known, so when it says 80%, about 80% of those answers should be correct, Typesafe claims.

Confidence becomes a routing rule. High, the system acts. Medium, it confirms first. Low, a person or a larger model takes over. Because Jev writes a number instead of text, Typesafe lists output as free and input at about $42 per billion tokens. LLMs charge more for output than for input.

But two weeks after Jev launched, OpenAI announced a Decisions API for the same job. It picks from predefined answers using text or images, where Jev takes text only. Clearly there is interest in this space.

If OpenAI follows Jev's pricing logic, small decisions that never justified a full LLM become candidates for automation at a fraction of the cost. This is significant, and I'm watching out for new usecases in this space.

author.about:
When payment systems fail, someone has to figure out what's broken, what it's going to hit, what can still move, and who needs to know right now. That's my job.

As a VP at JPMorgan Chase, I run the business incident management function for global payment operations - Fedwire, CHAPS, SWIFT, CHIPS, RTP, ACH. Our function is genuinely global: based in India, my team manages Fed opening at 9pm EST and CHAPS opening at 6am UK, alongside payment operations globally - we've hit peak volumes of 13 million transactions a day. My role is command and control: assessing blast radius, determining what can execute given available workarounds and capacity constraints, driving escalation and approvals at pace, and ensuring transparent communication across operations, technology, compliance, and executive leadership - simultaneously, under pressure, with regulatory SLAs on the clock.

My other discipline is enterprise resiliency - making sure that when something goes wrong at one of our 20+ global sites, people know what to do, know they're safe, and the work still moves. That means building the plans before the crisis, running the scenarios before the event, and being the steady voice when a natural disaster, power failure, or civil disruption makes the situation genuinely uncertain, making sure people aren't stranded, work doesn't stop, and someone who knows what they're doing is already on it before the situation becomes a crisis.

Running these systems at scale for long enough, you start to develop opinions about where human judgment is irreplaceable and where the surrounding infrastructure is just slow, manual, and overdue for rethinking. That curiosity is what pulled me into AI - and I built on it outside my role, because no one was going to hand it to me. Multi-agent orchestration with CrewAI. RAG pipelines with Pinecone. Workflow automation through n8n and GitHub Actions. MCP integrations. A creator intelligence product I'm currently building. I've run models locally, tested reasoning depth across model versions, and written about what I found. I co-developed and delivered LLM training curriculum internally at JPMorgan. I did all of this while running a 24x7 follow-the-sun operations function, because the intersection of AI capability and high-stakes regulated environments is where the genuinely hard problems live - and I don't find it easy to leave hard problems alone.

I started at Goldman Sachs in 2008. Years of high-stakes operations taught me what breaks, why, and what it costs. AI is changing the answers. The problems are getting more interesting.

posts.content:
Interviewer/Prospective Employer:

Can you tell me a bit more about what you did at your last job?

I was Office Manager. I did all general admin, sales, tenders, correspondence, reception, customer management, BOM, Petty Cash, Personnel time keeping/leave, vehicle maintenance, travel and stay bookings (no agent). Allocate payments, release orders. Make sure Customer and Supplier info stays updated. Ensure technical drawings stay updated and properly filed. (Hard and Soft Copy) Update any changes in technical drawings with comments. (Dated /reason). And more....

Reality of 1 order: 

⚙️ Operational Flow Chart: Step-by-Step
The chart above maps out the complete sequential path of your operational workflow. Below is the quick-reference checklist for each stage:

1. Inbound Inquiry & Costing

* Log RFQ: Register customer specifications, target dates, and destination country.
* Generate Quote: Calculate material, labour, margins, and state Incoterms and currency clearly.

2. Contract & Financial Initiation

* Establish Supply Contract: Lock down terms, milestones, and penalties.
* Receive & Allocate Payment:
* Local: Match EFT to pro-forma invoice.
   * Foreign: Route to CFC account, apply spot rate, and log FX variance.

3. Demand & Production Planning

* Create Sales Order (SO): Commit the order to the master schedule.
* Explode Bill of Materials (BOM): Run stock checks on multi-level components.
* Issue Purchase Orders (POs): Order missing parts from approved vendors.

4. Workshop Execution & Prioritisation

* Create WIP for Workshop: Open the work order, issue materials, and track labour.
* Prioritise Jobs: Score and sequence active jobs using this automated matrix:
* Priority 1: Penalties imminent or critical timeline → Immediate line clearance.
   * Priority 2: Standard contract jobs → Sequenced by component arrival dates.
   * Priority 3: Internal stock or low risk → Fills capacity gaps.

5. Quality Assurance & Compliance

* Complete Test Bay Reports: Sign off quality checkpoints, log serial numbers, and attach calibration data.

6. Export Preparation & Packaging

* Prepare Documentation: Compile Commercial Invoice, Packing List, and Certificate of Origin.
* Arrange Package/Pallets: Pack to destination country rules using certified ISPM 15 heat-treated wood.

7. Logistics & Dispatch

* Local Route: Issue a Delivery Note and dispatch via local courier.
* Export Route: Hand over goods and customs paperwork to the nominated freight forwarder; collect the Bill of Lading / Air Waybill.

posts.content:
Want an opener that books meetings?

Stop switching it every week. Do this instead:

Almost every rep I speak with is stuck on the same thing:

They change their approach every week.
So they never have enough data to see if their approach actually works.

So they decide it's broken.

That's the wrong approach.
You need DATA. Not feelings.

Here's the exact process I give my reps:

1. Pick 1 opener.
Permission-based, trigger-based, or both. Honestly, any of them will work.
If you've got a real trigger, use it. If not, go permission-based.

2. Rewrite it until it sounds like you.
Not like some LinkedIn opener from a sales director who hasn't dialled in 20 years.

3. Say it out loud 10 times and record it.
Yes, it's cringe. But you'll hear every filler word and every time you rush.

4. Use it unchanged for 20 conversations.
Not 20 dials. 20 conversations where they actually heard the opener.

5. Ask your question, then shut up.
They'll usually take 3 to 5 seconds to answer. Don't fill the silence.

6. Review 1 call a day.
Did you sound calm? Was it relevant? Did you end on a question, or just trail off?

7. Only change it after conversation 20.
3 bad calls tells you nothing. Neither does 5.
You need a real sample size to know if it works.

Any opener works once it sounds natural.
And it only sounds natural after you've said it enough times.

But If you're impatient (like me), I made a tool that'll tell you exactly how to book more meetings. Not "Dial more", actual advice tailored to you.

Try it here:

https://lnkd.in/euHgxvZ4

Save this for your next call block, and repost if you know a rep who needs it.

author.about:
I moved 5,000km from Ireland to Toronto with one goal: make money.

Started as an entry-level sales rep. Cold calling. 150+ dials a day.

9 months later: promoted to Account Manager.
6 months after that: promoted to Sales Manager.
6 months after that: Head of Sales. 24 years old. Youngest in the company's history.

I didn't get lucky. I got good at cold calling, and the results spoke for themselves.

When I started managing reps, I taught them the same things I used to get there. I've since coached 100+ B2B reps across 15 industries on how to cold call properly, handle objections without freezing, and book meetings consistently. Reps at HubSpot, Deel, Rippling, Oracle and Fortune 500 sales floors.

Now I run the Modern Seller Accelerator. Twelve weeks, for reps making 30+ calls a day.

We write your playbook with you on day one. Your opener, your objection responses, your discovery questions, built around the people you actually call. Then every week you send us a real call and we break it down line by line.

Weekly group coaching, one to one calls on your own market, and self-paced material covering every part of the call.

The promise: book 50% more meetings in 12 weeks, or you get your money back. Every cent.

I cap how many reps I take on at a time. Every one of them sends me a real call every week and gets it reviewed, and that only works at small numbers. When it's full, it's full.

Every spot starts with a free application call: https://modernseller.ai/schedule
